column3: Provides a broad causal backdrop: kufr and preference for dunya are paired with loss of guidance.
The mutual waiting scene is only a secondary parallel to opposed outcomes.
Defines a boundary against taking kuffar as awliya in place of the believers.
The fate of kuffar supplies a consequence-side parallel, including the channel's absent-shelter scene.
Shows divine support and firm footing for those who respond with support, making mawla active.
Directly joins Allah as mawla with nasir after others turn away.
Frames the believer-kafir divide through following haqq or batil, a backdrop to the contrast in 47:11.
The immediately preceding destruction of earlier deniers extends 47:11's consequence for kuffar.
Turning away offers a secondary route to forfeited proximity and support; it does not name mawla.
The haqq-batil contrast supports exclusive ultimate reliance, but only indirectly.
False protectors cannot help even themselves; this sharpens the limit of rival guardianship.
Its retained readings make an approaching, inescapable outcome a secondary contrast to sustaining closeness.
Reiterates the prior haqq-batil contrast without adding a distinct mawla relation.
Within the same conflict setting, divine agency preserves the deeds of those killed in His path.
Repetition continues the prior warning sequence but adds little beyond 75:34.
Denies that one mawla can avail another and denies help, setting a clear boundary on creaturely ties.
The same surah's repair of believers' condition supplies the positive side of its larger division.
Names Allah as mawla while resolving a binding obligation, joining authority, care, and support.
Its contrast in hostility and affection is a social parallel, not a direct mawla account.
The claim of collective self-help is a useful contrary parallel to dependable support.
The contrast link marks turning away after a covenant as boundary evidence only.
Again forbids taking kuffar as awliya instead of believers, though it is partly redundant with 3:28.
The same surah links rejection of what Allah sent to voided deeds, extending the negative side.
Its readings preserve succession and continuing responsibility as a secondary parallel to sustained guardianship.
Night and day alternation does not add a discernible mawla or support relation here.
Opens the surah's negative pattern of kufr and ruined deeds, supplying nearby context.
Contrasts mutual awliya among wrongdoers with Allah as wali of the muttaqin, including rival support networks.
Mawali here concerns inheritance allocation rather than the relation at issue in 47:11.
Obstruction and withdrawal from danger give only a channel-level parallel to failed group support.
The retained V12 route is contrast-only; the ayah adds no positive mawla evidence.
Supplies a loyal, steadfast believing group set against kuffar, a social background for allied support.
The same surah again connects hostile following and dislike of divine approval with voided deeds.
Turning away is a secondary image of leaving possible closeness, without a direct guardianship claim.
Explicitly denies any wali or nasir apart from Allah for the arrogant, matching 47:11's negative side.
The question of who guards through night and day develops protection as dependent rather than self-secured.
Turning away from the true account is a weak, indirect parallel to broken alignment.
Kufr and lack of guidance are broad background only, already supplied more directly above.
The same surah associates guidance with increase and taqwa, clarifying the believer side indirectly.
Directly states Allah as mawla and the best of helpers, strengthening the active-support reading.
Taking the disbelievers as allies is tied to lasting consequence, though the route is secondary.
The surah's declaration and forgiveness instruction offer only broad theological context.
Divine sovereignty over life and death frames the denial of any wali or nasir besides Allah.
Security after fear for believers and a contrary outcome for kufr offer an outcome-level parallel.
The permanent absence of wali and nasir gives a stark negative counterpart to 47:11.
Allah's awliya are marked by freedom from fear and grief, showing a lived consequence of affiliation.
The weakening of kafir plotting supplies a conflict-side expression of divine support.
The same surah's entry into jannah extends the favorable outcome for the believers.
Contrasts following revelation with taking other awliya, treating allegiance as practical direction.
Purification of believers and erasure of kuffar is relevant only as a general outcome contrast.
Taking rival awliya changes communal alignment; it is direct but overlaps earlier alliance-boundary ayat.
Affiliation with Allah, the Messenger, and believers yields a prevailing party, a group-support parallel.
Allah's defense of believers makes protection operative, though mawla is not named.
Repeats the same surah's ruined-deeds outcome for kuffar, with limited additional value.
Shows a rival authority becoming effective through repeated taking as wali, clarifying the danger of allegiance.
Reward for belief and righteous action is a general contrast but does not address guardianship.
Failed claims of belonging and ruined deeds offer only a remote contrary parallel.
The retained reading gives a secondary image of service and provision, not mawla.
The statement about fabricated falsehood does not add to the support relation.
Testing striving and patience is nearby context but does not illuminate mawla directly.
Forbids taking mockers and kuffar as awliya; it adds a specific but redundant boundary case.
Makes nearness to Ibrahim depend on following, while naming Allah wali of believers.
Names Allah, the Messenger, and believers as wali, placing guardianship within practiced communal affiliation.
Names Allah as wali in connection with repeated deeds and the abode of peace.
Betrayal and failed plotting do not supply a relevant mawla relation.
Its dunya and reward contrast is broad nearby context already expressed more directly.
Names Shaytan as wali through the acceptance of beautified deeds, a clear rival-allegiance trajectory.
The command against retreat in battle is only a distant support-related parallel.
Denies any wali or nasir besides Allah against harm or mercy, making protection non-independent.
Denies both wali and nasir besides Allah, but largely repeats the preceding direct pattern.
Turning away from obedience is a broad kufr marker rather than an account of mawla.
Exposed miserliness and rancor do not add a support or guardianship relation.
The denial of wali and nasir besides Allah is direct but redundant with 42:31 and 33:17.
Rejects seeking honor through kuffar as awliya and locates all honor with Allah.
Inability to repel the sudden event is a weak, channel-level parallel to failed protection.
Directly contrasts Allah's wilayah for believers with taghut awliya for kuffar and their opposed directions.
Change in divine favor gives a conditional backdrop, not a mawla relation.
Turning away and replacement stay within the surah's contrast but add little on guardianship.
The choice of Allah as wali is grounded in exclusive dependence on the creator and provider.
Truth of the Book and dispute do not add a discernible support relation.
The absence of strength or helper supplies a concise negative parallel to unsupported exposure.
Extends the awliya boundary even to family when kufr is preferred, while preserving kinship as distinct.
Distinguishing believers from hypocrites is only a general alignment parallel.
Retreat after guidance supplies nearby negative context but no guardian or helper relation.
The wrongdoers' lack of wali and nasir supplies a direct, though repetitive, negative counterpart.
Belief and taqwa alone do not add a specific mawla relation beyond earlier cards.
Non-control by the addressee is not evidence for the mawla relation; channel overlap is not localized.
Nearness and taqwa set a conflict boundary, a secondary parallel without mawla.
Turning away and Allah's sufficiency provide a broad outcome parallel only.
Secret coordination with those rejecting revelation adds the surah's contrary allegiance pattern.
Denies wali and nasir when social pressure displaces divine guidance, though it repeats the core boundary.
Prayer, taqwa, and gathering do not provide a distinct support relation here.
Allegiance to a condemned group without full belonging gives a nuanced contrary reading of affiliation.
Watching and patience do not supply a relevant mawla or support relation.
The closing plea names Allah as mawla and seeks nasr alongside mercy, forgiveness, and capacity.
Battlefield security and inward testing are a remote parallel, without a mawla relation.
Return to Allah as the true mawla frames guardianship as ultimate ownership and judgment.
Guidance and misguidance are broad theological context, not a specific support relation.
Names Allah as mawla and nasir alongside holding fast and sustained practice.
Shared worship, striving, and provision are general communal context rather than mawla evidence.
Promised mutual aid collapses under pressure, a concrete contrary image to dependable mawla support.
Explicitly denies any wali or nasir besides Allah, directly pairing guardianship with help.
Names Allah as wali when two believing groups falter, making the relation protective amid vulnerability.
Divine help and reliance show the operative support dimension of the relation without naming mawla.
Contrasts fear of Shaytan's allies with fear of Allah, preserving a rival-allegiance boundary.
Calls Allah sufficient as wali and nasir against enemies, an especially close parallel to 47:11.
The plea for a wali and nasir from Allah joins protection and aid in a setting of oppression.
Restricts taking others as awliya until a changed alignment, adding a boundary case.
Denies any wali or nasir besides Allah at the point of recompense.
Failure to believe is linked with taking them as awliya, a further contrary-allegiance pattern.
Denies a wali and intercessor besides Allah, extending the insufficiency of alternate refuge.
Likewise denies a wali and intercessor apart from Allah in the face of requital.
Treats taking Shayatin as awliya besides Allah as a misdirecting allegiance.
The prayer "أَنتَ وَلِيُّنَا" joins wilayah with forgiveness and mercy.
Names Allah as wali of the righteous and grounds that relation in revelation.
Those invoked besides Allah cannot render help or help themselves, clarifying failed rivals.
Describes believing emigrants and supporters as awliya to one another through shared action and aid.
States that kuffar are awliya of one another, an important counterpart to 47:11's denial.
Makes believing men and women awliya of one another through shared moral and devotional practice.
Returns every soul to Allah as its true mawla, framing ultimate guardianship and judgment.
No one can remove divine harm or withhold His good, an active-protection parallel.
Denies any awliya besides Allah and presents their inability to escape consequence.
Forbids leaning toward wrongdoers and denies awliya besides Allah, followed by the loss of help.
Addresses Allah as wali in dunya and akhirah, directly extending the continuity reading.
Challenges the taking of awliya that cannot benefit or harm themselves, exposing rival impotence.
Denies any wali or defender against Allah when guidance is displaced by desires.
One whom Allah leaves astray finds no wali besides Him, linking wilayah with guidance.
Denies a guiding wali to one left astray, a secondary guidance-side reading.
Places true walayah with Allah alone and contrasts outcomes under His authority.
Depicts kuffar taking Allah's servants as awliya, a contrary-allegiance pattern.
Warns against becoming a wali of Shaytan, preserving a rival-proximity reading.
Portrays divine protection as unanswerable, a support parallel without the wali term.
The denial of taking awliya besides Allah gives only an indirect parallel from another speaker's perspective.
The parable of awliya besides Allah as a fragile house sharply depicts false shelter.
Denies any wali or intercessor besides Allah after affirming His governance.
Those taken as gods cannot help their adherents, a failed-support counterpart.
Records claims that other awliya bring nearness to Allah, preserving a competing allegiance claim without endorsing it.
Allah's sufficiency for His servant supplies an active-support parallel.
Denies any protector from Allah at the point of flight and reversal.
The awliya in dunya and akhirah preserve a distinct continuity-and-support reading.
Allah's watching over those who take other awliya supplies a boundary, not positive support.
Contrasts taking other awliya with Allah as the wali who gives life to the dead.
One left astray by Allah has no wali after Him, linking guardianship and direction.
Denies awliya who can help besides Allah, pairing both terms in the contrary case.
Distinguishes hostile awliya from the muttaqin, a relational outcome parallel.
Denies any awliya besides Allah for one who rejects the divine caller.
The immediate continuation contrasts believers' garden-entry with kafir enjoyment and the Fire.
The same local sequence joins destruction of stronger communities with absence of a helper.
Directly contrasts one upon clear proof from his Lord with one following evil work and desire.
Calls believers to obedience and warns against voided deeds, extending the surah's alignment condition.
Continues the surah's account of kufr and obstruction through its final consequence.
Names the Fire as mawla for the hypocrites and kuffar, a severe contrary designation to preserve alongside 47:11.
Allah's support of the faithful with a spirit gives an operative support parallel.
Forbids taking Allah's enemies as awliya while they oppose faith, a direct allegiance boundary.
Specifies the hostile conduct that makes taking such parties as awliya wrongful.
Names Allah as mawla and places divine, angelic, and believing support in a coordinated scene.
Denies any refuge apart from Allah, a close but non-wali expression of dependence.
